note: Fair baseline: one direct prompt, full policy, full dossier.

cases.title: Cancelled short-notice flight, crew shortage
cases.rationale: The passenger held a confirmed booking (S1.2(a)) and the flight was cancelled before check‑in opened (S1.2(b)), so the claim is in scope and qualifies as a cancellation (S2.1(a)). The operational record shows crew unavailability, a carrier‑controlled cause (S3.2(b)). Notice was less than 7 days with no re‑routing offer, so 100% of the band B amount (420 units) applies (S4.2, S5.1). Duty of care is owed but no receipts are submitted, and proof of acceptance for travel is missing, making evidence insufficient.

cases.title: Weather cancellation with overnight duty of care
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and qualifies due to a cancelled flight (S2.1(a)). The operational record shows the cancellation was caused by weather below operating minima at OSL, an extraordinary cause (S3.3(a)), so no Part 5 compensation is payable (S3.1). Duty of care is owed regardless of cause (S6.1) and the passenger provided itemised receipts for hotel and meals, totalling 240 units within the 300-unit cap (S6.2, S6.3). Evidence is sufficient, and the carrier's denial of duty‑care reimbursement is challengeable (S9.1).

cases.title: Unforeseen technical fault, six-hour delay, long haul
cases.rationale: The passenger had a confirmed booking, presented for check-in, and the claim is assumed timely (in scope). The flight arrived 6h06m late, exceeding the 3h30m threshold, so it qualifies as a delay disruption. The operational record shows an unscheduled technical fault found by the carrier's own maintenance, making the cause carrier-controlled and compensation payable. Distance of 6,635 km places the claim in band C (750 units); the delay exceeds 5 hours, so no taper applies, and Part 4 notice reductions do not apply to delays. Duty of care is owed for the >2‑hour wait, but no receipts are provided, so reimbursement is zero pending evidence.

cases.title: Missed connection on one booking, tapered delay
cases.rationale: The passenger held a confirmed booking, presented for check-in, and filed within 18 months (implied), making the claim in scope. The arrival at Sydney was 4h10m later than scheduled, exceeding the 3h30 threshold under S2.1(b), so the disruption qualifies. The delay was caused by a late inbound aircraft due to MT ground handling shortfall, a carrier-controlled cause under S3.2(e). Distance MAD‑SYD is 17,680 km (band C, 750 units); the delay of 4h10m triggers the 50 % taper of S5.4, yielding 375 units compensation. Duty of care may be owed but itemised receipts are missing, so evidence is insufficient to quantify it.

cases.title: Missed connection across two separate bookings
cases.rationale: The passenger's bookings were separate, so under S2.3 the missed connection does not qualify as a disruption under Part 2. The delay of the first leg is carrier‑controlled (crew positioning delay), but without evidence of timely check‑in and claim filing we cannot confirm S1.2, making the claim's scope uncertain. Consequently, no compensation or duty of care is payable, and the missing evidence must be requested.

cases.title: Twelve days notice with a compliant re-routing offer
cases.rationale: The claim lacks evidence of when it was filed, so scope cannot be determined. However, the flight was cancelled 12 days before departure due to commercial consolidation (carrier‑controlled), and the carrier offered re‑routing departing 1 hour early and arriving 3.5 hours late, which falls within the 7‑20‑day notice re‑routing exemption, so no Part 5 compensation would be payable even if the claim were in scope. Duty of care and downgrade reimbursement are not owed.

cases.title: Fourteen days notice, non-compliant re-route, exact band boundary
cases.rationale: The flight was cancelled due to a carrier‑controlled IT system failure (crew rostering). With 14 days’ notice, the 7‑20 day notice band applies, giving 50% of the Band A amount (180 × 0.5 = 90). Duty‑of‑care reimbursement requires itemised receipts, which are missing, and the claim filing date is not on file, so evidence is insufficient.

cases.title: Cancellation with twenty-five days notice
cases.rationale: The booking confirmation shows a confirmed reservation and the carrier notification indicates the flight was cancelled well before check‑in opened, satisfying S1.2(a) and (b). However, the claim filing date is missing, so S1.2(c) cannot be verified, leaving scope uncertain. The cancellation qualifies as a disruption under S2.1(a) and the cause is a commercial schedule decision, which is carrier‑controlled per S3.2(d). Notice was given more than 21 days prior, so under S4.2 no compensation is payable. Evidence of acceptance for travel and the claim filing date are absent, making the record insufficient to decide.

cases.title: Delay claim with no arrival-time evidence
cases.rationale: The claim lacks evidence of when it was filed (needed to assess S1.2(c)) and of the actual arrival time at Doha (needed to assess S2.1(b)). While the operational record shows a carrier‑controlled technical delay, without proof of arrival delay ≥3h30 min we cannot determine if the disruption qualifies or if compensation is due.

cases.title: Cancellation with no notification timestamp
cases.rationale: The claim is for a cancelled flight (S2.1(a)), so it qualifies as a disruption. The operational record shows crew sickness, which is carrier‑controlled under S3.2(b). However, evidence is lacking for the passenger’s acceptance for travel, the cancellation notification timestamp (needed to apply the notice ladder), and receipts for any duty‑care expenses, making the claim insufficiently evidenced to determine scope, compensation, or duty of care.

cases.title: Contradictory arrival times across three documents
cases.rationale: The claim's filing date is unknown, so in_scope cannot be confirmed. The actual arrival time conflicts between the carrier's letter (1h55m delay) and the passenger's photo (5h35m delay), preventing a determination of whether the delay meets the 3h30m threshold for qualification. Duty of care cannot be paid without itemised receipts. Therefore evidence is insufficient and the appropriate next step is to request the missing items.

cases.title: Rejection citing weather contradicted by the operational record
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and qualifies as a cancellation. The operational record shows crew duty (carrier-controlled), not weather, so compensation is payable. Notice was less than 7 days with no re-routing offer, yielding 100% of the Band B amount (420 units). However, evidence of passenger acceptance for travel and duty‑of‑care receipts is missing, so the claim cannot be finalised without those items.

cases.title: Rejection that is correct and must not be challenged
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope because the passenger held a confirmed booking and the flight was cancelled before check-in opened, and the claim was filed well within 18 months. The cancellation qualifies as a disruption under S2.1(a). The operational record shows the cancellation was due to weather below operating minima at Edinburgh, which is an extraordinary cause under S3.3(a), so no compensation is payable. However, evidence of the passenger's acceptance for travel (boarding pass, check-in confirmation, or denied-boarding notice) is missing, making the record insufficient to decide; therefore the appropriate next step is to request that evidence.

cases.title: Angry passenger demanding premature escalation
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and involves a carrier-controlled cancellation, but evidence is missing to prove the passenger was accepted for travel and to substantiate any duty-of-care expenses. Without these, compensation and duty-of-care amounts cannot be determined.

cases.title: Challenge ignored for thirty-five days, escalation ripe
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope because the passenger had a confirmed boarding, presented for check-in, and filed within 18 months. The flight arrived 7h42m late, qualifying under S2.1(b). The operational record shows a carrier‑controlled technical fault (S3.2(a)), so compensation under Part 5 is payable at the Band C rate of 750 units. Duty of care is owed but cannot be assessed without itemised receipts, making the evidence insufficient.

cases.title: Partial settlement: duty of care paid, compensation wrongly refused
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and qualifies as a cancellation. The operational record shows a carrier-controlled IT outage, not weather, so compensation is payable. With less than 7 days notice and the offered re-routing failing the exemption, the full 420 units compensation is due; duty of care of 300 units was already paid and evidence is sufficient, so the passenger should challenge the carrier's refusal of compensation.

cases.title: Involuntary downgrade with no delay and no cancellation
cases.rationale: The passenger holds a confirmed booking and presented for check-in, satisfying S1.2(a) and (b); the claim filing date is unknown, so in_scope cannot be determined. No cancellation, delay ≥3h30, or denied boarding occurred, so the disruption does not qualify under Part 2. However, an involuntary downgrade from business to economy entitles the passenger to 40% of the fare paid (800 units) under S7.1, yielding 320 units of downgrade reimbursement.

cases.title: Extraordinary cause with forty hours to recover
cases.rationale: The booking is confirmed and the flight was cancelled before check-in opened, satisfying S1.2; the cancellation qualifies under S2.1(a). The bird strike is extraordinary but the carrier had spare aircraft and >12 hours to recover, making the cause carrier-controlled per S3.5. With less than 7 days notice and no re-routing offer, 100% of the Band B compensation (420 units) applies under S4.2 and S5.1. Evidence of acceptance for travel and duty-of-care receipts is missing, so the claim is not yet evidence‑sufficient and the next step is to request those items.

cases.title: Fleet-wide airworthiness directive, duty of care only
cases.rationale: The claim lacks evidence of when it was filed, so the in‑scope requirement of S1.2(c) cannot be settled. The flight was cancelled, which qualifies as a disruption under S2.1(a). The cause is a regulator‑notified manufacturing defect, making it extraordinary under S3.3(g) and S3.4, thus no compensation is payable; duty of care of 180 units is supported by itemised receipts.

cases.title: Passenger overstates the delay; evidence shows just under threshold
cases.rationale: The claim's filing time is unknown, so S1.2(c) cannot be verified, making in_scope indeterminate. The arrival record shows a 3h20m delay, but the passenger states at least six hours, creating a contradiction on the fact needed to assess qualification under S2.1(b). Without resolving these, qualification, compensation, and duty of care cannot be determined.

cases.title: Decisive fact buried at document eight of nine
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope and qualifies as a cancelled flight. The disruption was carrier‑controlled (crew duty limit breach). However, the carrier offered re‑routing departing within 1 hour before and arriving within 2 hours after the original flight, triggering the S4.4 re‑routing exemption, so no Part 5 compensation is payable. Evidence is sufficient and no duty‑of‑care expenses are shown.

cases.title: Two composed reductions at an exact band boundary
cases.rationale: The claim meets S1.2(a) and (b) but lacks evidence of filing date, so in_scope cannot be determined. The flight arrived 3h45m late, qualifying under S2.1(b). The operational record shows a late inbound aircraft due to engineering hold, a carrier-controlled cause under S3.2(a). Compensation would be 420 units band B, tapered to 50% for a 3h30m–5h delay, yielding 210 units, but cannot be finalised without confirming the claim is in scope and duty‑of‑care entitlement. Evidence is missing for the claim filing timestamp and wait‑time details needed to assess duty of care, so the claim is not evidence‑sufficient.

cases.title: Rejection resting on a re-routing offer that is not in the record
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope because the passenger had a confirmed booking, the flight was cancelled before check-in, and the claim was filed within 18 months. It qualifies as a cancellation under S2.1(a). The operational record shows a commercial consolidation (COM-CONS), which is carrier-controlled under S3.2(d). Evidence is lacking for proof of acceptance for travel and any re-routing offer, preventing determination of whether the re-routing exemption applies and thus whether compensation is payable.

cases.title: Strong claim filed nineteen months late
cases.rationale: The claim was filed 19 months and 8 days after the scheduled departure, exceeding the 18‑month limit in S1.2(c), so it is out of scope per S1.3. The flight was cancelled due to a carrier‑controlled technical fault (S3.2(a)), qualifying as a disruption under S2.1(a). Because the claim is out of scope, no compensation, duty of care, or downgrade reimbursement is payable.

cases.title: Receipts with a non-reimbursable item and a cap

derivation: S3.3(b) airspace closure by the air navigation service provider, not caused by the carrier -> extraordinary
S3.5 does not apply: the closure was still in force at the scheduled departure time
S6.1 duty of care is owed regardless of cause
S6.2(b) hotel 210.00 and airport transfer 21.00 are reimbursable
Replacement clothing is not among the categories in S6.2 and is not reimbursable, so 95.00 is excluded
S6.3 the cap is 300 units per passenger per disruption -> 300 units payable
S6.4 itemised receipts are present for every line

cases.title: Denied boarding, four hours late, no taper
cases.rationale: The claim satisfies S1.2(a) and (b) but lacks evidence of timely filing under S1.2(c), making in_scope indeterminate. The passenger was involuntarily denied boarding due to overbooking (carrier‑controlled) and arrived 4h20m late, so the disruption qualifies under S2.1(b) and (c). Compensation is the Band B amount of 420 units with no reductions; duty of care cannot be paid without receipts.

cases.title: Stated cause contradicted by the record, where the policy resolves it
cases.rationale: The claim's timeliness (within 18 months) cannot be verified without evidence of when it was filed, leaving in_scope undeterminable. The flight was cancelled due to crew sickness, a carrier‑controlled cause, making the disruption qualify under S2.1(a). With less than 7 days notice and no qualifying re‑routing offer, the passenger is owed the full band B compensation of 420 units; no duty‑of‑care or downgrade expenses were incurred.

cases.title: Settlement offer that matches the full entitlement
cases.rationale: The claim is in scope because the passenger held a confirmed booking, presented for check-in before the cancellation, and filed within 18 months. The flight cancellation qualifies as a disruption, and the cause is carrier-controlled (VT flight-planning system outage). Compensation is 420 units (band B, <7 days notice, no re-routing exemption) and duty of care is 170 units (receipted hotel and meals), matching the carrier's settlement offer of 590 units, which should be accepted.
